title: Journaling for anxiety: write it down, then check it

description: How to journal for anxiety: note each worry in one line, then check it that evening. In trials, about 9 in 10 feared outcomes never happened.
dek: Getting the worry out of your head is the first half. The half that changes things is coming back to see what actually happened.

faq.a: Yes, modestly. A 2023 meta-analysis of 31 trials found a small effect of expressive writing on depression, anxiety, and stress that showed up at follow-up. Journaling that tracks whether worries came true has done better than simply recording thoughts in trials with people who have generalized anxiety.

faq.q: How do you journal for anxiety?
faq.a: During the day, write each worry as one line with a prediction and a 0 to 100 likelihood. In the evening, read each line and note whether it happened, how you coped, and whether there is one step you can take tomorrow.

It can if you write the same fear in more detail every night without new information. Expressive writing often lowers mood right after a session, and one study of recently separated adults found it hurt people who were stuck searching for meaning. Shorter entries, outcome-checking questions, and writing about yourself in the third person help.

faq.q: What should I write in an anxiety journal?
faq.a: Write the prediction in plain words, how likely it feels, and how upset you are. Useful prompts include what the evidence for and against is, what you would do first if it happened, and what you would tell a friend who wrote it.

faq.q: Should I journal before bed if anxiety keeps me awake?
faq.a: A short, specific to-do list before bed helped people fall asleep faster in a 2018 sleep-lab study. Do the longer review of your worries earlier in the evening, not while lying in the dark.

informationGain: Unlike the top results, which stop at getting worries onto the page, this piece builds its method on the Worry Outcome Journal trials (including a 2026 RCT) showing that checking worries against what actually happened beats plain thought recording, with about 9 in 10 feared outcomes never occurring.
